# From Module 2

Module 2 used limma to produce two lists of DEGs, using 6 normal samples as controls: Favorable vs. Control and Unfavorable vs. Control. This module takes the DEGs of both lists together and asks how they **regulate each other** in three conditions: Favorable tumors, Unfavorable tumors and normal kidney. Comparing the three networks, we look for the hub regulators of each condition and, finally, for a candidate therapeutic biomarker specific to Unfavorable Wilms tumor.

**Session plan:** why a ranked list isn't the end of the story → gene regulatory networks → building the three networks → overlapping the networks: shared edges and hubs → Unfavorable-specific biomarker → closing pediatric lens.

# Part 1 — Why a Ranked Gene List Isn't the End of the Story

Module 2 answered one question, gene by gene: *is this gene expressed differently in the tumor than in normal kidney?* That question treats every gene in isolation — it says nothing about whether two candidate genes **influence each other**, or sit in entirely separate pathways.

**Reframing the arc:** Module 2 found candidates by asking "is this gene behaving abnormally compared to normal kidney?" Module 3 asks a different question about those same candidates: **"how do they work together, and does that change between the two histology groups?"** A single gene's p-value cannot answer that as It requires looking at the candidate genes **as a system**, which is exactly what a gene regulatory network does.

<div class="alert-info">
**What we're building toward.** We will infer **three** separate networks over the same panel of Module 2's DEGs: one using the 82 favorable-histology tumors, one using the 42 unfavorable-histology tumors, and one using the 6 normal samples as a **baseline network**. We then overlap them to find which regulators are hubs in which condition, and look for a hub that is **specific to Unfavorable tumors**: a candidate biomarker.
</div>

# Part 2 — Gene Regulatory Networks in Plain Language

A **gene regulatory network (GRN)** is just a diagram: each **node** is a gene, and an **edge** between two genes means "knowing one gene's expression level helps predict the other's across these samples".

# Part 3 — Building the Three Networks

We now infer three real networks, **Favorable**, **Unfavorable** and **Control**, over the **same set of genes**, so that they can be compared edge by edge and hub by hub.

## Step 1 — The Gene Panel: Strong DEGs from Both Comparisons

The panel comes straight from Module 2: the **union** of the DEGs of *Favorable vs Control* and *Unfavorable vs Control*, i.e. every gene that is a DEG in at least one of the two comparisons, whatever its category (shared, Favorable-only or Unfavorable-only).

GENIE3 grows one random forest per gene, so a network over all of them would take hours, far too long to run live. We therefore keep only the **strong DEGs: |log2FC| > 3** (at least an 8-fold change versus normal kidney) in at least one comparison.

```{r load-data, echo=TRUE}
de_favorable_vs_control   <- read_csv("results/differential_expression_favorable_vs_control.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
de_unfavorable_vs_control <- read_csv("results/differential_expression_unfavorable_vs_control.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

tumor_tpm_raw <- read_csv("data/TARGET_WT_gene_expression_tpm.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  rename(gene_symbol = gene_name)
control_tpm_raw <- read_csv("data/TARGET_WT_control_gene_expression_tpm.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  rename(gene_symbol = gene_name)
sample_metadata <- read_csv("data/sample_metadata.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Curated list of 1,639 human transcription factors (Lambert et al., Cell 2018).
human_tfs <- readLines("data/human_transcription_factors_Lambert2018.txt")
```

```{r build-panel, echo=TRUE}
panel_log2fc_cutoff <- 3

strong_degs <- function(de_table) {
  de_table %>% filter(status != "Not DEG", abs(log2FC) > panel_log2fc_cutoff) %>% pull(gene_symbol)
}

strong_favorable   <- strong_degs(de_favorable_vs_control)
strong_unfavorable <- strong_degs(de_unfavorable_vs_control)
panel_genes        <- union(strong_favorable, strong_unfavorable)

# Only transcription factors are allowed to act as regulators (see below).
panel_tfs <- intersect(panel_genes, human_tfs)
```

```{r table-panel}
datatable(
  tibble(
    gene_set = c("Strong DEGs, Favorable vs Control", "Strong DEGs, Unfavorable vs Control",
                 "Strong DEGs in both", "Panel (union)", "Transcription factors in the panel"),
    genes    = c(length(strong_favorable), length(strong_unfavorable),
                 length(intersect(strong_favorable, strong_unfavorable)), length(panel_genes), length(panel_tfs))
  ),
  rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", ordering = FALSE),
  caption = "The shared gene panel used for all three networks (|log2FC| > 3)."
)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Why only transcription factors as regulators?** GENIE3 can in principle let every gene predict every other gene, but that is both slow and biologically loose: the genes that actually *regulate* the expression of other genes are mainly **transcription factors (TFs)**, proteins that bind DNA and switch genes on or off. So we give GENIE3 the `regulators = panel_tfs` argument: every panel gene is a possible **target**, but only the `r length(panel_tfs)` TFs of the panel can be **regulators**. This is standard practice in network inference, and it makes the run about ten times faster. A consequence to keep in mind: **only TFs can become hubs**.
</div>

## Step 2 — One Expression Matrix per Condition

```{r build-matrices, echo=TRUE}
# Genes x samples matrix of log2(TPM + 1) for the panel, from a TPM table.
panel_matrix <- function(tpm_table, sample_ids) {
  m <- as.matrix(tpm_table[, sample_ids])
  rownames(m) <- tpm_table$gene_symbol
  log2(m[panel_genes, ] + 1)
}

favorable_ids   <- sample_metadata %>% filter(histologic_subtype == "Favorable")   %>% pull(case_submitter_id)
unfavorable_ids <- sample_metadata %>% filter(histologic_subtype == "Unfavorable") %>% pull(case_submitter_id)

matrix_favorable   <- panel_matrix(tumor_tpm_raw, favorable_ids)
matrix_unfavorable <- panel_matrix(tumor_tpm_raw, unfavorable_ids)
matrix_control     <- panel_matrix(control_tpm_raw, colnames(control_tpm_raw)[-1])
```

```{r table-matrices}
datatable(
  tibble(
    condition = c("Favorable", "Unfavorable", "Control"),
    genes     = c(nrow(matrix_favorable), nrow(matrix_unfavorable), nrow(matrix_control)),
    samples   = c(ncol(matrix_favorable), ncol(matrix_unfavorable), ncol(matrix_control))
  ),
  rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", ordering = FALSE),
  caption = "Input matrices: same genes, different samples."
)
```

## Step 3 — Running GENIE3 in Each Condition

```{r run-genie3, echo=TRUE}
#nTrees = 500 (default 1000) keeps the run short.
run_genie3 <- function(expr_matrix) {
  set.seed(20261013)
  GENIE3(expr_matrix, regulators = panel_tfs, nTrees = 500, nCores = 1, verbose = FALSE)
}

weights_favorable   <- run_genie3(matrix_favorable)
weights_unfavorable <- run_genie3(matrix_unfavorable)
weights_control     <- run_genie3(matrix_control)
```

GENIE3 returns a weight for every TF → target pair: how useful that TF was for predicting that target. Almost all weights are tiny; we keep the **300 strongest edges** of each network.

```{r build-edge-lists, echo=TRUE}
n_top_edges <- 300

top_edges <- function(weights) {
  getLinkList(weights) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    mutate(regulatoryGene = as.character(regulatoryGene), targetGene = as.character(targetGene)) %>%
    arrange(desc(weight)) %>%
    slice_head(n = n_top_edges)
}

edges_favorable   <- top_edges(weights_favorable)
edges_unfavorable <- top_edges(weights_unfavorable)
edges_control     <- top_edges(weights_control)

dir.create("results", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_csv(edges_favorable,   "results/gene_network_favorable_edges.csv")
write_csv(edges_unfavorable, "results/gene_network_unfavorable_edges.csv")
write_csv(edges_control,     "results/gene_network_control_edges.csv")
```

```{r table-edges}
datatable(
  bind_rows(Favorable = edges_favorable, Unfavorable = edges_unfavorable, Control = edges_control, .id = "network") %>%
    mutate(weight = signif(weight, 3)),
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel"), pageLength = 10),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "Top 300 edges (TF → target) of each network."
)
```

## Step 4 — Visualizing the Three Networks

In the plots below each **node** is a gene and each **arrow** goes from a TF to one of its predicted targets. **Diamonds are TFs**, dots are targets. Node colors show the gene's category from Module 2's UpSet plot:

- **red**: up in both tumor subtypes vs normal kidney; **blue**: down in both;
- **purple**: DEG only in Unfavorable; **orange**: DEG only in Favorable.

Node size grows with the number of targets (the bigger, the more hub-like). Hover a node to highlight its direct connections, or pick a gene from the dropdown.

```{r network-plot-function, echo=TRUE}
gene_category <- full_join(
  de_favorable_vs_control   %>% select(id = gene_symbol, fav = status),
  de_unfavorable_vs_control %>% select(id = gene_symbol, unf = status),
  by = "id"
) %>%
  filter(id %in% panel_genes) %>%
  mutate(category = case_when(
    fav == "Up"   & unf == "Up"   ~ "Shared up",
    fav == "Down" & unf == "Down" ~ "Shared down",
    fav == "Not DEG"              ~ "Unfavorable only",
    unf == "Not DEG"              ~ "Favorable only",
    TRUE                          ~ "Opposite direction"
  ))

category_colors <- c(`Shared up` = "#e74c3c", `Shared down` = "#2980b9",
                     `Unfavorable only` = "#8e44ad", `Favorable only` = "#e67e22",
                     `Opposite direction` = "#7f8c8d")

plot_network <- function(edges, title) {
  out_degree <- count(edges, regulatoryGene, name = "n_targets")
  nodes <- tibble(id = unique(c(edges$regulatoryGene, edges$targetGene))) %>%
    left_join(gene_category, by = "id") %>%
    left_join(out_degree, by = c(id = "regulatoryGene")) %>%
    mutate(
      n_targets = replace_na(n_targets, 0),
      label = id,
      shape = if_else(id %in% panel_tfs, "diamond", "dot"),
      color = category_colors[category],
      size  = 10 + 2 * n_targets,
      title = paste0(id, "<br>", category, "<br>targets: ", n_targets)
    )

  visNetwork(nodes, edges %>% transmute(from = regulatoryGene, to = targetGene),
             main = title, height = "600px", width = "100%") %>%
    visEdges(arrows = "to", color = list(color = "#bdc3c7", opacity = 0.6)) %>%
    visOptions(highlightNearest = TRUE, nodesIdSelection = TRUE) %>%
    # Layout computed once in R (seeded), physics off: fast and identical on every knit.
    visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr", randomSeed = 1, physics = FALSE)
}
```

```{r plot-network-favorable}
plot_network(edges_favorable, "Favorable network (82 tumors)")
```

```{r plot-network-unfavorable}
plot_network(edges_unfavorable, "Unfavorable network (42 tumors)")
```

### The Control Network: Read With Real Caution

```{r plot-network-control}
plot_network(edges_control, "Control network (6 normal kidney samples)")
```

# Part 4 — Overlapping the Networks

With three networks over the same genes, we can compare them directly at two levels: **edges** (are the same TF → target links found?) and **hubs** (are the same TFs the most connected?).

## Shared Edges

```{r edge-overlap, echo=TRUE}
edge_ids <- function(edges) paste(edges$regulatoryGene, "→", edges$targetGene)

edge_sets <- list(Favorable = edge_ids(edges_favorable),
                  Unfavorable = edge_ids(edges_unfavorable),
                  Control = edge_ids(edges_control))

edge_overlap <- combn(names(edge_sets), 2, simplify = FALSE) %>%
  map_dfr(function(pair) {
    a <- edge_sets[[pair[1]]]; b <- edge_sets[[pair[2]]]
    tibble(networks = paste(pair, collapse = " vs "),
           shared_edges = length(intersect(a, b)),
           jaccard = round(length(intersect(a, b)) / length(union(a, b)), 3))
  })
```

```{r table-edge-overlap}
datatable(
  edge_overlap,
  rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = "t", ordering = FALSE),
  caption = "Shared top-300 edges between networks. Jaccard index = shared edges / all distinct edges of the two networks (0 = nothing in common, 1 = identical)."
)
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Reading this table.** The two tumor networks share more edges with each other than either does with the control network: their strongest regulatory links are not the ones present in normal kidney. Part of the disagreement with the control network is real rewiring, but part is simply noise from its 6 samples; this table cannot tell the two apart.
</div>

## Hub Genes in Each Network

A TF's **out-degree** is the number of targets it has among the network's top 300 edges: the more targets, the more hub-like the TF. The table lists every TF of the panel with its out-degree in all three networks.

```{r hub-table, echo=TRUE}
hub_table <- bind_rows(Favorable = edges_favorable, Unfavorable = edges_unfavorable,
                       Control = edges_control, .id = "network") %>%
  count(network, regulatoryGene, name = "out_degree") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = network, values_from = out_degree, values_fill = 0) %>%
  right_join(tibble(regulatoryGene = panel_tfs), by = "regulatoryGene") %>%
  mutate(across(c(Favorable, Unfavorable, Control), ~ replace_na(.x, 0))) %>%
  select(TF = regulatoryGene, Control, Favorable, Unfavorable) %>%
  arrange(desc(Unfavorable))

write_csv(hub_table, "results/gene_network_hub_comparison.csv")
```

```{r table-hubs}
datatable(
  hub_table,
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel"), pageLength = 10),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "Out-degree (number of targets in the top 300 edges) of every panel TF in each network."
)
```

To compare the networks at a glance, we take the **top 10 hubs** of each network (ties at the 10th place are all kept) and plot their out-degree in all three conditions.

```{r plot-hubs, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
top_hubs <- hub_table %>%
  pivot_longer(-TF, names_to = "network", values_to = "out_degree") %>%
  group_by(network) %>%
  slice_max(out_degree, n = 10, with_ties = TRUE) %>%
  filter(out_degree > 0) %>%
  pull(TF) %>%
  unique()

hub_table %>%
  filter(TF %in% top_hubs) %>%
  pivot_longer(-TF, names_to = "network", values_to = "out_degree") %>%
  mutate(network = factor(network, levels = c("Control", "Favorable", "Unfavorable")),
         TF = fct_reorder(TF, out_degree, .fun = max)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = out_degree, y = TF, fill = network)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Control = "#7f8c8d", Favorable = "#2980b9", Unfavorable = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(x = "Out-degree (targets in the top 300 edges)", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       title = "Top hub TFs of each network, compared across the three conditions") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

<div class="alert-info">
**What to look for.** A TF with a long bar in **all three** colors is a hub everywhere: probably a general feature of this gene panel. A TF with a long **red** bar and short blue and gray bars is a hub **only in Unfavorable tumors**: a candidate for regulatory rewiring specific to anaplastic histology. That is exactly what Part 5 looks for.
</div>

# Part 5 — Toward an Unfavorable-Specific Therapeutic Biomarker

The clinical question: **is there a regulator that becomes a hub specifically in anaplastic (Unfavorable) Wilms tumor, having more targets there than in either Favorable or Control?** We focus on **gains only**: a TF whose regulatory role is newly active in Unfavorable is a more directly actionable candidate than one that merely loses a role it has elsewhere.

```{r candidate-ranking, echo=TRUE}
candidates <- hub_table %>%
  mutate(hub_specificity = Unfavorable - pmax(Favorable, Control)) %>%
  filter(hub_specificity > 0) %>%
  arrange(desc(hub_specificity))

top5_candidates <- candidates %>% slice_head(n = 5)
```

```{r table-candidates}
datatable(
  candidates %>%
    select(TF, Control, Favorable, Unfavorable, hub_specificity) %>%
    slice_head(n = 15),
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel"), pageLength = 10),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "Top 15 panel TFs gained as hubs in Unfavorable (hub_specificity > 0), ranked by hub_specificity. The top 5 are plotted below."
)
```

## Shortlist: Top 5 Candidates, Side by Side


```{r plot-candidate-shortlist, fig.width=15, fig.height=5}
tumor_tpm <- as.matrix(tumor_tpm_raw[, -1])
rownames(tumor_tpm) <- tumor_tpm_raw$gene_symbol
tumor_groups <- factor(sample_metadata$histologic_subtype[match(colnames(tumor_tpm), sample_metadata$case_submitter_id)])

gene_expr_by_group <- function(gene) {
  bind_rows(
    tibble(TF = gene, group = "Control",
           log2_tpm = log2(unlist(control_tpm_raw[control_tpm_raw$gene_symbol == gene, -1]) + 1)),
    tibble(TF = gene, group = as.character(tumor_groups),
           log2_tpm = log2(tumor_tpm[gene, ] + 1))
  )
}

shortlist_expr <- map_dfr(top5_candidates$TF, gene_expr_by_group) %>%
  mutate(
    group = factor(group, levels = c("Control", "Favorable", "Unfavorable")),
    TF    = factor(TF, levels = top5_candidates$TF)
  )

ggplot(shortlist_expr, aes(x = group, y = log2_tpm, fill = group)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.35, trim = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, size = 1, alpha = 0.6) +
  stat_compare_means(comparisons = list(c("Control", "Unfavorable"), c("Favorable", "Unfavorable")),
                      method = "wilcox.test", label = "p.signif", size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ TF, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Control = "#7f8c8d", Favorable = "#2980b9", Unfavorable = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log2(TPM + 1)", fill = NULL,
       title = "Top 5 candidates by |hub_specificity|: expression across groups") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Reading this panel.** Each facet is one TF's `log2(TPM + 1)` in Control / Favorable / Unfavorable (gray / blue / red, left to right in every panel). Significance brackets compare Unfavorable against Control and against Favorable. A convincing candidate should show both a real network signal **and** a plausible expression pattern.

Pick one from this shortlist and the next step will build its full subnetwork, direct-target table, and a sourced pathway write-up.
</div>

## A Closer Look: E2F1

**E2F1** is the chosen candidate: `r candidates %>% filter(TF == "E2F1") %>% pull(Unfavorable)` targets in Unfavorable versus `r candidates %>% filter(TF == "E2F1") %>% pull(Favorable)` in Favorable and `r candidates %>% filter(TF == "E2F1") %>% pull(Control)` in Control. The question that matters most for interpretation: **are the connections E2F1 gained specifically in Unfavorable tumors — the ones it does *not* have in Favorable or Control — genes with a real, independent cancer link?**

```{r e2f1-targets, echo=TRUE}
candidate_gene <- "E2F1"

e2f1_targets <- bind_rows(Favorable = edges_favorable, Unfavorable = edges_unfavorable, Control = edges_control, .id = "network") %>%
  filter(regulatoryGene == candidate_gene) %>%
  select(network, targetGene, weight)

targets_elsewhere <- e2f1_targets %>% filter(network != "Unfavorable") %>% pull(targetGene) %>% unique()

e2f1_targets_annotated <- e2f1_targets %>%
  filter(network == "Unfavorable") %>%
  mutate(new_in_unfavorable = !targetGene %in% targets_elsewhere) %>%
  arrange(desc(weight))

n_new_targets <- sum(e2f1_targets_annotated$new_in_unfavorable)
```

```{r table-e2f1-targets}
datatable(
  e2f1_targets_annotated %>% mutate(weight = signif(weight, 3)),
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel"), pageLength = 10),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "E2F1's targets in the Unfavorable network, flagged where that specific link is new (absent from both the Favorable and Control top-300 edge lists)."
)
```

`r n_new_targets` of E2F1's `r nrow(e2f1_targets_annotated)` Unfavorable targets are new in exactly this sense.

```{r plot-e2f1-subnetwork}
plot_network(edges_unfavorable %>% filter(regulatoryGene == candidate_gene),
             "E2F1 and its targets in the Unfavorable network")
```

### Are the New Connections Cancer-Related?

**E2F1 itself is a well-established cancer gene** — the RB-pathway's main activator of G1/S cell-cycle entry, with higher expression predicting shorter survival in several adult cancers (e.g. breast). First, the expression of its 15 Unfavorable-specific targets, across all three groups:

```{r plot-e2f1-new-targets-expr, fig.width=15, fig.height=10}
new_targets <- e2f1_targets_annotated %>% filter(new_in_unfavorable) %>% pull(targetGene)

new_targets_expr <- map_dfr(new_targets, gene_expr_by_group) %>%
  rename(gene_symbol = TF) %>%
  mutate(
    group       = factor(group, levels = c("Control", "Favorable", "Unfavorable")),
    gene_symbol = factor(gene_symbol, levels = new_targets)
  )

ggplot(new_targets_expr, aes(x = group, y = log2_tpm, fill = group)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.35, trim = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.08, size = 0.7, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_compare_means(comparisons = list(c("Control", "Unfavorable"), c("Favorable", "Unfavorable")),
                      method = "wilcox.test", label = "p.signif", size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ gene_symbol, ncol = 5, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Control = "#7f8c8d", Favorable = "#2980b9", Unfavorable = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log2(TPM + 1)", fill = NULL,
       title = "E2F1's 15 new Unfavorable-specific targets: expression across groups") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.x = element_blank(), axis.ticks.x = element_blank())
```

Of those 15, the ones actually worth a second look are the ones where **Favorable vs. Unfavorable itself** is significant in the panel above, not just "present as a network edge in Unfavorable," but a real expression difference between the two tumor subtypes directly:

```{r table-fav-vs-unf-significant, echo=TRUE}
fav_vs_unf_significance <- new_targets_expr %>%
  filter(group %in% c("Favorable", "Unfavorable")) %>%
  group_by(gene_symbol) %>%
  summarise(
    p_value             = wilcox.test(log2_tpm ~ group)$p.value,
    median_favorable    = round(median(log2_tpm[group == "Favorable"]), 2),
    median_unfavorable  = round(median(log2_tpm[group == "Unfavorable"]), 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    higher_in = if_else(median_unfavorable > median_favorable, "Unfavorable", "Favorable"),
    p_value   = signif(p_value, 3)
  ) %>%
  filter(p_value < 0.05) %>%
  arrange(p_value)
```

```{r table-fav-vs-unf-sig-display}
datatable(
  fav_vs_unf_significance,
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel"), pageLength = 15),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = paste0(nrow(fav_vs_unf_significance), " of 15 new targets with a significant Favorable-vs-Unfavorable expression difference (Wilcoxon, p < 0.05).")
)
```

Then the literature on each of all 15 genes, with rows that have a documented cancer role highlighted:

```{r table-cancer-roles, echo=TRUE}
gene_cancer_roles <- tribble(
  ~gene_symbol, ~function_summary,                                  ~cancer_relevance,
  "MKI67",  "Proliferation antigen (Ki-67)",                        "Standard clinical proliferation marker; correlates with tumor stage and histologic subtype in Wilms tumor itself (Juric 2010, n=48; Krishna 2016, n=31)",
  "KIF4A",  "Mitotic kinesin, chromosome segregation",               "Member of a 2022 E2F-target prognostic signature in prostate cancer (with MXD3, PLK1, EPHA10); high-risk score predicts poor outcome and therapy resistance",
  "BUB1B",  "Spindle-assembly-checkpoint kinase",                    "Near-universally upregulated across 33 TCGA cancer types; expression tracks with worse progression/prognosis in most",
  "MCM2",   "DNA replication licensing factor",                      "Canonical E2F/S-phase target; replication-licensing genes are repeatedly tied to tumor proliferation rate",
  "SMC4",   "Condensin complex subunit (chromosome condensation)",   "Same condensin family as NCAPH, a hub found in an earlier version of this analysis; condensin overexpression broadly tied to proliferative tumors",
  "NCAPG",  "Condensin I complex subunit (chromosome condensation)", "Same condensin family as SMC4/NCAPH; reported overexpressed in several adult cancers",
  "SKA3",   "Kinetochore-microtubule attachment",                    "Spindle/kinetochore gene; dysregulation tied to chromosomal instability, a recognized driver of tumor progression",
  "CDCA5",  "Sororin (sister-chromatid cohesion)",                   "Cohesion regulator reported overexpressed in several solid tumors, tracking with proliferation",
  "GTSE1",  "G2/M regulator, p53-linked",                            "Modulates p53 stability/localization; implicated in mitotic-exit control relevant to tumor checkpoints",
  "BLM",    "Bloom syndrome helicase (genome stability)",            "Loss causes Bloom syndrome, a cancer-predisposition disorder; maintains replication-fork stability",
  "TICRR",  "Replication-origin firing / checkpoint",                "Regulates DNA replication timing; replication-stress genes are a recognized cancer-vulnerability class",
  "CRACD",  "Actin-capping regulator, WNT pathway",                  "Reported TUMOR SUPPRESSOR in colorectal cancer and small-cell lung cancer (opposite direction from every other gene in this table)",
  "AFF2",   "Transcriptional elongation factor",                     "Limited cancer literature -- mainly studied in fragile-X-related conditions",
  "RCOR2",  "REST corepressor complex, chromatin",                   "Limited cancer literature -- linked to stem-cell/pluripotency programs in some contexts",
  "GDF11",  "TGF-beta superfamily ligand",                           "Limited cancer literature -- mixed pro-/anti-proliferative roles reported, not clearly established"
) %>%
  mutate(cancer_related = !startsWith(cancer_relevance, "Limited"))

datatable(
  gene_cancer_roles,
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(
    dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel"), pageLength = 15,
    columnDefs = list(list(visible = FALSE, targets = 3))
  ),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "Each of E2F1's 15 new Unfavorable-specific targets, with its documented role in cancer. Rows highlighted in red have a documented cancer role."
) %>%
  formatStyle(
    "gene_symbol", "cancer_related",
    target = "row",
    backgroundColor = styleEqual(c(TRUE, FALSE), c("#fdecea", "white"))
  )
```

<div class="alert-info">
**Bottom line.** 12 of the 15 new targets (highlighted above) have a documented cancer role — 11 as part of E2F1's own canonical DNA-replication/mitosis program (the textbook machinery it switches on for S-phase), one (`CRACD`) as a tumor suppressor pointing the *opposite* direction. This network recovered E2F1 specifically to its own well-known target program, without being told what those genes were. This is itself a reassuring sign the signal is real, not noise. Still a **candidate, not a biomarker**: this needs a stable result under re-sampling, independent-cohort validation, and evidence the pathway is druggable before any clinical claim.
</div>

## Is E2F1 a Druggable Biomarker?

We query **DGIdb** (the Drug Gene Interaction Database, [dgidb.org](https://dgidb.org)) for E2F1 and all 15 new Unfavorable-specific targets at once, and ask it directly: does *any* drug, approved or experimental, have a recorded interaction with each of these genes?

```{r query-dgidb, echo=TRUE}
dgidb_genes <- c(candidate_gene, new_targets)

dgidb_query <- sprintf(
  '{ genes(names: [%s]) { nodes { name interactions { drug { name approved } } } } }',
  paste0('"', dgidb_genes, '"', collapse = ",")
)

dgidb_response <- tryCatch(
  POST("https://dgidb.org/api/graphql", body = list(query = dgidb_query), encode = "json", timeout(10)),
  error = function(e) e
)

# Distinguish "the live call failed" from "the call worked and genuinely
# found nothing" -- an all-zero chart means two very different things
# depending on which happened, and only one of them is a real result.
dgidb_query_ok <- !inherits(dgidb_response, "error") && status_code(dgidb_response) == 200
dgidb_failure_reason <- if (inherits(dgidb_response, "error")) {
  paste("Request failed:", conditionMessage(dgidb_response))
} else if (!dgidb_query_ok) {
  paste("DGIdb returned HTTP", status_code(dgidb_response))
} else {
  NA_character_
}

dgidb_nodes <- if (dgidb_query_ok) {
  content(dgidb_response, as = "parsed", simplifyVector = TRUE)$data$genes$nodes
} else {
  NULL
}

dgidb_per_gene <- if (!is.null(dgidb_nodes) && nrow(dgidb_nodes) > 0) {
  map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(dgidb_nodes)), function(i) {
    ints <- dgidb_nodes$interactions[[i]]
    # Unique drug names, approved drugs first -- kept as a list-column so
    # the full name list survives the later join/arrange, not just a count.
    drug_names <- if (is.null(ints) || nrow(ints) == 0) {
      character(0)
    } else {
      tibble(name = ints$drug$name, approved = ints$drug$approved) %>%
        distinct(name, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
        arrange(desc(approved)) %>%
        pull(name)
    }
    tibble(
      gene_symbol    = dgidb_nodes$name[i],
      n_interactions = if (is.null(ints)) 0L else nrow(ints),
      n_approved     = if (is.null(ints)) 0L else sum(ints$drug$approved, na.rm = TRUE),
      drug_names     = list(drug_names)
    )
  })
} else {
  tibble(gene_symbol = character(), n_interactions = integer(), n_approved = integer(),
         drug_names = vector("list", 0))
}

dgidb_counts <- tibble(gene_symbol = dgidb_genes) %>%
  left_join(dgidb_per_gene, by = "gene_symbol") %>%
  mutate(
    n_interactions = replace_na(n_interactions, 0L),
    n_approved     = replace_na(n_approved, 0L),
    drug_names     = map(drug_names, ~ if (is.null(.x)) character(0) else .x)
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_interactions))
```

```{r dgidb-query-status}
# Printed regardless of outcome, so a failed live call is never mistaken
# for a genuine "no drug interactions exist" result.
if (dgidb_query_ok) {
  cat("DGIdb query succeeded:", sum(dgidb_counts$n_interactions > 0), "of", nrow(dgidb_counts),
      "genes have at least one recorded interaction.\n")
} else {
  cat("DGIdb query FAILED in this session --", dgidb_failure_reason,
      "\nThe chart and numbers below are from this machine's live result where available;",
      "if every count reads 0, that reflects this network call failing here, not a real finding.",
      "This needs outbound internet access to dgidb.org from wherever the Rmd is knit",
      "(Binder sessions normally have this; a fully offline or heavily firewalled environment will not).\n")
}
```

```{r plot-dgidb, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.5, eval=dgidb_query_ok}
p_dgidb <- dgidb_counts %>%
  mutate(gene_symbol = fct_reorder(gene_symbol, n_interactions),
         is_candidate = gene_symbol == candidate_gene) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = gene_symbol, y = n_interactions, fill = is_candidate,
             text = paste0(gene_symbol, ": ", n_interactions, " recorded drug interactions (",
                           n_approved, " involving an approved drug)"))) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#e74c3c", `FALSE` = "#2980b9"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Drug-gene interactions recorded in DGIdb",
       title = "E2F1 (red) vs. its 15 new Unfavorable-specific targets: known druggability") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

ggplotly(p_dgidb, tooltip = "text")
```

```{r table-dgidb, eval=dgidb_query_ok}
datatable(
  dgidb_counts,
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel"), pageLength = 16),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "Real DGIdb interaction counts, queried live: every gene with 0 recorded interactions has no known drug-gene data in the database, not a failed lookup."
)
```

The top 3 genes by recorded interaction count, with the actual drug names behind that count (approved drugs listed first; capped at 10 names per gene since some genes have dozens):

```{r table-top3-drugs, echo=TRUE, eval=dgidb_query_ok}
top3_drugs <- dgidb_counts %>%
  slice_head(n = 3) %>%
  mutate(
    drug_names_shown = map_chr(drug_names, function(names) {
      if (length(names) == 0) return("(none)")
      shown <- if (length(names) > 10) names[1:10] else names
      label <- paste(shown, collapse = ", ")
      if (length(names) > 10) paste0(label, ", ... (", length(names) - 10, " more)") else label
    })
  ) %>%
  select(gene_symbol, n_interactions, n_approved, drug_names_shown)
```

```{r table-top3-drugs-display, eval=dgidb_query_ok}
datatable(
  top3_drugs,
  extensions = "Buttons",
  options = list(dom = "Bfrtip", buttons = c("csv", "excel"), pageLength = 3),
  rownames = FALSE,
  caption = "Real drug names from DGIdb for the top 3 most-targetable genes in this panel."
)
```

# Part 6 — Closing Pediatric Lens

Pediatric rare disease means two things at once: **very few samples**, and a **uniquely sensitive population** to try to collect more from. That combination is exactly why a result like E2F1's matters here — with only `r ncol(matrix_unfavorable)` Unfavorable tumors and `r ncol(matrix_control)` real controls to work with, and essentially no realistic way to get many more, finding and correctly flagging a candidate target in the data that already exists is as important as it gets.
